title: Ukraine's Robot Offensive Reclaims Donetsk Villages as Winter Approaches
excerpt: Explosives-packed BTR-60s driven by remote control helped Ukraine retake villages in Donetsk, while an ex-minister's new "Army of Robots" project promises to mechanise the war's deadliest jobs.
body:
• Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps packed Soviet-era BTR-60 armoured carriers with explosives and drove them by remote control into Russian fortifications near the village of Nove on Sept. 28, as part of Operation Vivaldi in northern Donetsk.
  • Kyiv says the offensive liberated Nove, Ridkodub and Katerynivka, captured 250 Russian troops and freed 125 square kilometres of territory — claims Moscow has not confirmed.
  • Former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov separately launched an "Army of Robots" initiative on Sept. 26, aiming to shift the war's most dangerous jobs from soldiers to machines.
  • With mud season and shorter days arriving, the tempo of fighting on both sides is expected to slow through October into winter.

Ukraine has turned some of its oldest military hardware into some of its newest: Soviet-era BTR-60 armoured personnel carriers, packed with explosives and stripped of their crews, have been driven by remote control into Russian defensive positions near the village of Nove in the Donetsk region.

The unmanned assaults were detailed by Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps on Sept. 28 as part of Operation Vivaldi, a phased counteroffensive along the Lyman axis. A reconnaissance drone hovered overhead throughout each mission, relaying live video to operators who steered the eight-wheeled carriers — vehicles built in the 1960s — straight into some of the most heavily fortified Russian positions in the sector. One of the old machines was so battle-worn it was no longer fit for normal combat; instead of abandoning it, engineers fitted cameras, a remote-control system and a full load of explosives.

"They were used to blow up the enemy's strongest fortifications,"

— Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps

Deception paved the way

The robot strike was only the visible tip of the operation. Before the assault, Ukrainian forces ran an elaborate electronic deception campaign: fake radio traffic suggested the real attack would come along the Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna axis, drawing Russian reinforcements into what corps commander Biletskyi described as pointless counterattacks while electronic jamming blinded Russian sensors to the actual movement toward Nove. Ukrainian reporting suggests two explosive-laden BTRs were used in total, and that Russian defenders initially mistook the approaching vehicles for their own reinforcements.

Nove sits on high ground commanding a bridgehead over the Siverskyi Donets river toward Lyman, the region's major railway hub. By the end of the week, the 3rd Army Corps said it had also liberated Ridkodub and Katerynivka and restored control near Novomykhailivka and Lypove, claiming 125 square kilometres retaken across the two phases of Vivaldi and more than 2,000 Russian troops killed or wounded in the latest phase. It said 250 Russian troops surrendered, including officers, artillerymen and drone operators, whom Kyiv hopes to exchange for Ukrainian prisoners of war. None of these claims have been independently verified.

A broader robotisation of the war

The BTR attacks build on Ukraine's fast-expanding use of ground robots. According to Ukraine's defence ministry, unmanned ground vehicles carried out more than 25,000 logistics and casualty-evacuation missions in August alone, taking the year's total to roughly 112,000, while the defence procurement agency said more than 22,000 UGVs had been contracted by July 2026 — nearly double the number contracted in all of 2025. Compact ground robots fitted with automatic grenade launchers took part in the opening assaults at Nove, and the corps said its heavy bomber drones had delivered suicide ground drones more than 10 kilometres behind Russian lines for the first time.

Two days before the Nove strike, former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov — the architect of Ukraine's earlier "Army of Drones" programme — launched a new "Army of Robots" initiative. Fedorov, who left the defence ministry in July, said the project is an ecosystem rather than a single company, aimed at getting machines to take over evacuating the wounded, delivering ammunition, mining and demining, reconnaissance and holding positions. He set an ambitious target: a humanoid robot killing a Russian soldier within six months. Analysts noted that the futuristic machines shown in the launch video were conceptual, AI-generated renders rather than fielded systems — the practical battlefield use of Ukraine's ground robots remains considerably more advanced than its humanoid designs.

Winter looms over the gains

The gains remain modest against the map of the whole war: Russia still controls roughly 45,000 square miles of Ukraine, about 20 per cent of the country, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. And the calendar is working against both sides. Military analysts expect the tempo of operations to slow further through October as autumn mud and shorter days arrive, with the eastern front typically grinding toward static, attritional fighting by November. Whether Ukraine's robotic edge can compensate for its manpower disadvantage in winter conditions — when drones struggle with cold, snow and low visibility — will be the next real test of Operation Vivaldi's playbook.

For the Indian diaspora, the operation is a measure of the war's trajectory rather than a direct concern: India's balanced posture on the conflict, the war's continuing drag on global energy and food prices, and the safety of the remaining Indian nationals in Ukraine all turn on how long the fighting lasts and at what intensity.
